site.nav.label: Site
site.lang.label: Language
site.foot.about: Gadfly Exams is a spoken examination platform for universities and training providers, made by MindAttic.
site.meta.imageAlt: Gadfly Exams: an engraving of a gadfly beside the words Oral exams that follow up on what the student said.
site.landing.metaTitle: Gadfly Exams: spoken exams that follow up on what the student said
site.landing.metaDescription: Gadfly Exams asks questions out loud, in English, Korean or Spanish, and writes every follow-up from the student's previous answer, so understanding shows in the reasoning. A human grades and approves every result.
site.landing.hero.title: Exams that find out whether a student understands.
site.landing.hero.lede: When anyone can paste a question into an AI, a correct answer proves very little. Gadfly's examiner asks out loud, then follows up on the student's own words: why, what if, and whether two things they said can both be true.
site.landing.plate.alt: One of Gadfly's two examiners, shown live and silent.
site.landing.plate.a1: It's what you give up when you choose something, <mark>like the money you spend</mark>.
site.landing.plate.q2: You said <mark>like the money you spend</mark>. If a concert ticket were free, would going still cost you anything?
site.landing.plate.a2: I suppose the evening. I could have worked a shift.
site.landing.plate.q3: So is it the money, or the best thing you gave up? Can both be true?
site.landing.plate.caption: An illustration of the questioning, not a recorded exam. Each follow-up is written from the answer before it.
site.landing.why.title: Why one right answer isn't enough
site.landing.why.intro: A single correct answer can be recalled, guessed or pasted. Gadfly asks the questions a good examiner asks in person.
site.landing.why.p1: It starts with "what is it?", then asks the student to explain their answer, defend it against a case that doesn't fit, and use it somewhere new. That is much harder to do without understanding the idea.
site.landing.why.p2: Each follow-up is written from the previous answer, so it can't be looked up or prepared in advance. Understanding shows in the reasoning, not in the wording, and an unclear answer gets a neutral clarifying question that never hints at the answer.
site.landing.why.p3: Instructors use their own course material. Gadfly turns it into learning objectives and rubrics they can edit, and every question and judgment cites the passage it rests on.
site.landing.feel.title: A conversation, not a form
site.landing.feel.intro: The exam is meant to feel like talking with a calm, attentive examiner, in the student's own language, without anything working against them.
site.landing.feel.talk.title: An examiner who keeps pace.
site.landing.feel.talk.body: The examiner acknowledges each answer at once and starts the next question while it is still being written, a checked sentence at a time. A finished answer goes in after about two seconds of silence. The full panel of AI models still judges every answer in the background.
site.landing.feel.languages.title: English, Korean and Spanish, side by side.
site.landing.feel.languages.body: An exam can be offered in all three. The student chooses before beginning, and the examiner listens, speaks and lip-syncs in that language. Exam texts are translated by machine and approved by the instructor; graders read the original words. Every score on a Korean or Spanish exam needs a person's approval until a bilingual calibration shows the AI panel agrees with human graders.
site.landing.feel.esl.title: Graded on content, not accent.
site.landing.feel.esl.body: Students say which language they speak best; nothing is guessed from a voice or a name. A student answering in a second language gets longer pauses before an answer is taken, a slightly slower examiner, and a short question about a word the recognizer was unsure of instead of a misjudged answer.
site.landing.feel.ready.title: A get-ready studio.
site.landing.feel.ready.body: One screen to choose the exam language, the camera and microphone, and the examiner (there are two, one female and one male), to test them and to read a short sentence so the examiner hears you well. A free practice run with the same examiner stores nothing.
site.landing.feel.gaze.title: Looking away to think is fine.
site.landing.feel.gaze.body: Nothing reacts while a student is thinking before they answer, and anywhere on the screen counts as looking at it. Students don't watch themselves during the exam. Leaving the exam window pauses it; a person, not the software, decides whether anything needs following up.
site.landing.feel.access.title: Built for WCAG 2.2 AA.
site.landing.feel.access.body: Keyboard-operable exam controls, captions for every question, a choice of how long a silence waits, and a light, high-contrast design checked on desktop and phone. Our accessibility statement says what is still to be tested.
site.landing.path.title: From the first question to a released grade
site.landing.path.intro: A person stays accountable for every result. Nothing reaches a student until someone with authority approves it.
site.landing.path.s1.title: The instructor uploads course material
site.landing.path.s1.body: Text, Markdown, PDF, Word, EPUB or HTML. Gadfly drafts the concepts and rubrics; the instructor corrects and approves them.
site.landing.path.s2.title: The student answers out loud, on camera
site.landing.path.s2.body: A talking examiner asks each question with captions, in English, Korean or Spanish, and the conversation appears as a transcript beside the examiner.
site.landing.path.s3.title: A panel of AI models scores each objective
site.landing.path.s3.body: Models from different families score against the rubric and the cited material. Their grade is preliminary.
site.landing.path.s4.title: An examiner grades independently
site.landing.path.s4.body: Blind by default, without seeing the AI's view. Large disagreements go to a second reviewer to reconcile.
site.landing.path.s5.title: An authorized person approves the result
site.landing.path.s5.body: Only then is it published to the student, with appeals and amendments kept on the record.
site.landing.wont.title: What Gadfly will not do
site.landing.wont.intro: The research on proctoring, attention and AI grading sets clear limits. Gadfly is built inside them.
site.landing.wont.cheat.title: Decide that a student cheated.
site.landing.wont.cheat.body: Signals such as a face out of view or a tab switch are low-confidence notes for a reviewer. They are never a verdict and never part of the grade.
site.landing.wont.cancel.title: Cancel an exam or delete results automatically.
site.landing.wont.cancel.body: Leaving the exam window pauses the exam and keeps the words already said. Repeated or long absences mark the attempt for an instructor to review, with the student's own explanation. Results and transcripts are always kept.
site.landing.wont.video.title: Store or send video.
site.landing.wont.video.body: Camera checks run in the student's browser. Video frames never leave the device; only short descriptions of events are sent.
site.landing.wont.accent.title: Mark anyone down for accent or fluency.
site.landing.wont.accent.body: Judges are told to ignore transcription slips, filler words and false starts. Pauses and speech rate never enter the grade.
site.landing.wont.guess.title: Guess a student's language or background.
site.landing.wont.guess.body: Students state the languages they speak. Gadfly never infers them from a voice, an accent, a name or a face, and graders are not shown them.
site.landing.wont.detector.title: Run an AI-text detector.
site.landing.wont.detector.body: Those tools are unreliable and flag non-native writers. Answer style is context for the reviewer only.
site.landing.wont.claim.title: Claim more than it has measured.
site.landing.wont.claim.body: Gadfly makes no validity claims until its own pilot measures them.
site.landing.science.title: An old method, examined carefully
site.landing.science.body: Gadfly follows the Socratic elenchus and Piaget's clinical interview, and says plainly where the research stops.
site.landing.science.quote: "This man thinks he knows something when he does not."
site.landing.closing.title: See it with your own course material
site.landing.closing.body: We'll set up a demonstration on a topic you teach and walk your team through grading and review.
site.how.metaDescription: Before, during and after a Gadfly exam: course material to rubrics, a spoken exam with a talking examiner in English, Korean or Spanish, then AI scoring, blind human grading and approval.
site.how.title: How a Gadfly exam works
site.how.lede: Instructors bring their material, students talk with the examiner, and people decide the grade.
site.how.before.title: Before the exam
site.how.before.upload.title: Upload course material.
site.how.before.upload.body: Text, Markdown, PDF, Word, EPUB or HTML, up to 20 MB a file.
site.how.before.concepts.title: Review the concept map.
site.how.before.concepts.body: Gadfly drafts the concepts and the links between them, each with citations to the passages it came from. Fix anything wrong or missing.
site.how.before.rubrics.title: Set objectives and rubrics.
site.how.before.rubrics.body: Rubric criteria have level descriptors from 0 to 5, and they are versioned.
site.how.before.policy.title: Lock the grading policy.
site.how.before.policy.body: How AI and human grades combine, and how large a disagreement must be before it goes to reconciliation.
site.how.before.languages.title: Choose the exam's languages.
site.how.before.languages.body: English, Korean and Spanish are on by default, and you can turn any of them off. Gadfly drafts the exam's title, instructions and objective titles in Korean and Spanish by machine; you edit and approve them. The course material and rubric stay as written, so every language is the same exam.
site.how.before.assign.title: Assign the exam.
site.how.before.assign.body: To students in your organization, with a time limit, extra time where needed, and a signed launch link if you start exams from another system.
site.how.during.title: During the exam
site.how.during.ready.title: A get-ready studio first.
site.how.during.ready.body: One screen in the student's language: the exam language, their camera and microphone with a check of each, the examiner they'd like (female or male), and an optional short reading so the examiner hears them well. A free practice run with the same examiner is one click away.
site.how.during.consent.title: A plain consent notice.
site.how.during.consent.body: It says what is recorded, that video stays on the device, how long data is kept, that the camera only checks presence and never grades or decides, and that a person decides the grade.
site.how.during.examiner.title: A spoken examiner.
site.how.during.examiner.body: A talking head asks each question with captions, in the exam's language, with lip-sync for English, Korean and Spanish. With reduced motion she stays live with gentler movement; without 3D graphics, her glowing circuitry sphere speaks instead.
site.how.during.answer.title: The student answers aloud.
site.how.during.answer.body: Each answer is taken as heard, with no read-back or do-over, so the exchange stays real-time; words the recognizer was unsure of are marked for the reviewer.
site.how.during.pace.title: A conversational pace.
site.how.during.pace.body: The examiner acknowledges each answer at once and starts speaking the next question while it is still being written, each sentence checked so it gives nothing away. While thinking, the examiner glances aside and says a short line instead of leaving a silence.
site.how.during.followUps.title: Follow-ups from their own words.
site.how.during.followUps.body: Clarify, probe, counterexample, apply to a new situation, and "can both be true?" when two claims conflict. "I don't know" is recorded as an honest answer.
site.how.during.rephrase.title: Repeat or say it another way.
site.how.during.rephrase.body: A student can ask the examiner to repeat a question or to word it differently. The rewording is checked like any question and never counts against them.
site.how.during.gaze.title: Room to think.
site.how.during.gaze.body: Looking away while working out an answer is normal, so nothing reacts before the first word. Only a long look off the screen while answering gets a gentle reminder, from the examiner first. Students don't see themselves during the exam, just a small camera-on sign.
site.how.during.window.title: Leaving the window pauses the exam.
site.how.during.window.body: The examiner stops and the words already said are kept. On return the examiner picks up the question. Repeated or long absences mark the attempt for an instructor to review, with the student's explanation; nothing is cancelled automatically.
site.how.during.clock.title: A fair clock.
site.how.during.clock.body: It starts when the examiner asks the first question, and pauses if the camera, microphone or connection drops.
site.how.after.title: After the exam
site.how.after.ai.title: AI scores, marked preliminary.
site.how.after.ai.body: A panel of models scores each objective against the rubric and the cited material.
site.how.after.blind.title: Blind human grading.
site.how.after.blind.body: An examiner grades without seeing the AI's view, by default.
site.how.after.reconcile.title: Reconciliation.
site.how.after.reconcile.body: Large gaps between AI and human go to a second reviewer.
site.how.after.approve.title: Approval, then release.
site.how.after.approve.body: Nothing reaches a student until an authorized person approves it. Appeals and amendments stay on the record.
site.how.after.original.title: The original words are the record.
site.how.after.original.body: A Korean or Spanish exam is graded from the student's answers in that language against the same rubric. Graders can ask for a machine translation into English, labelled as such and never stored as the record.
site.how.after.fairness.title: Fairness you can check.
site.how.after.fairness.body: Owners and admins can compare AI and human grades by accommodation, by exam language and by the language students said they speak best. Small groups are never shown.
site.how.after.reports.title: Review and reports.
site.how.after.reports.body: A timeline of every question, answer, citation and judge's verdict, with Markdown, CSV and PDF reports and course analytics.
site.how.languages.title: English, Korean, Spanish, and students between languages
site.how.languages.p1: A Korean or Spanish exam is heard by a recognizer for that language, spoken and lip-synced in it, and the examiner asks questions in it from the same course material and rubric; in Spanish it uses neutral Latin American Spanish and addresses the student as usted. The student pages, the exam room, the practice run, the emails and the get-ready page are in Korean and Spanish too. Every score on a Korean or Spanish exam needs a person's approval until a bilingual calibration shows the AI panel agrees with human graders, and a native Spanish-speaking tester has not yet checked the Spanish.
site.how.languages.p2: When the language a student speaks best differs from the exam's, the examiner adapts quietly: waiting longer before taking an answer, speaking a little slower and more plainly, and asking about a word that may have been misheard. The AI judges read what the answer says, without filler words and false starts, and are never told why. A student taking an exam in the language they speak best gets the standard exam.
site.how.record.title: The record stays intact
site.how.record.body: Every answer is kept exactly as the student gave it. A typed answer's clarifications and typo fixes are added beside the original, never in place of it, and the audit trail is append-only. Reviewers see integrity notes, such as a long look away from the screen or a second voice, as low-confidence context. Graders working blind don't see them at all.
site.how.roles.title: Who does what
site.how.roles.owner.name: Owner and Admin
site.how.roles.owner.does: Manage members and invitations, retention, cost limits, API keys, webhooks and usage for the organization.
site.how.roles.instructor.name: Instructor
site.how.roles.instructor.does: Upload material, build assessments and exams, approve their translations, assign them, and review sessions.
site.how.roles.examiner.name: Examiner
site.how.roles.examiner.does: Grade sessions independently, blind to the AI's view by default.
site.how.roles.reviewer.name: Second reviewer
site.how.roles.reviewer.does: Reconcile large disagreements between the AI panel and the examiner.
site.how.roles.student.name: Student
site.how.roles.student.does: Take assigned exams and read released results.
site.how.it.title: For your IT and data teams
site.how.it.tenant: Each institution is its own organization; every database query is limited to it.
site.how.it.signIn: Staff sign in with two-step verification. Passwords are hashed with Argon2id, with lockout after repeated failures.
site.how.it.api: An API with organization keys, signed launch links and signed webhooks, described by an OpenAPI document, and LTI 1.3 for Canvas, Moodle, Blackboard Learn and D2L Brightspace.
site.how.it.retention: Retention periods, per-student data export and erasure. See the privacy notice and the security page.

site.pricing.faq.title: Questions
site.pricing.faq.prices.a: The cost of running an exam depends on its length and on the AI providers it uses, and institutions buy in very different ways. We'd rather quote a price that fits your term dates and volume than publish one that doesn't.
site.pricing.faq.exam.a: One student's attempt at an assigned exam.
site.pricing.faq.seat.a: An account with any staff role: owner, admin, instructor, examiner or second reviewer. Students are counted separately.
site.pricing.faq.trial.q: Can we try it before we commit?
site.pricing.faq.trial.a: Yes. A trial gives one course team its own organization for 30 days, and we help you set up the first exam on your material.
site.pricing.faq.install.q: Do students need to install anything?
site.pricing.faq.install.a: No. Exams run in a current web browser with a camera and a microphone.
site.pricing.faq.languages.q: Which languages can students take an exam in?
site.pricing.faq.languages.a: English, Korean and Spanish, on every plan. You choose which languages each exam is offered in and approve its translated texts. Korean and Spanish scores need a person's approval until a bilingual calibration shows the AI panel agrees with human graders.
site.pricing.faq.secondLanguage.q: Are students who speak English as a second language at a disadvantage?
site.pricing.faq.secondLanguage.a: Gadfly is built not to mark anyone down for accent, grammar or fluency. Students who say English isn't the language they speak best get more time before an answer is taken, a slightly slower examiner and a check on words that may have been misheard, and you can compare AI and human grades by language. These settings are reasoned from research and have not yet been tuned in a pilot.
site.pricing.faq.lookAway.q: Will a student be penalized for looking away?
site.pricing.faq.lookAway.a: No. Looking away to think is normal and never affects the grade. A long look off the screen while answering gets a gentle reminder from the examiner, and anything the camera notices is a note for a person to weigh.
site.pricing.faq.access.a: We build to WCAG 2.2 AA and run automated checks on every page, but haven't yet tested with screen readers or had a formal audit, so we don't claim conformance. Instructors can grant extra time, typed answers, an eye-contact accommodation and a window-absence accommodation.
site.science.metaDescription: Why follow-up questions built from a student's own answers say more about understanding, where the method stops working, and what Gadfly does about each limit, from attention to second-language speakers.
site.science.title: The science behind Gadfly
site.science.lede: What the Socratic method is, why follow-up questions reveal understanding, and where the research sets limits.
site.science.elenchus.title: Asking until the answers have to hold together
site.science.elenchus.body: In Plato's Apology, Socrates questions a man reputed to be wise and finds that he "thinks he knows something when he does not" (21d). He calls himself a gadfly, stinging a sluggish horse awake (30e). Scholars call his way of questioning the elenchus. Two features of it carry straight into Gadfly:
site.science.elenchus.own: Only the student's own words count. The examiner works from what the student actually said, not from premises it supplied.
site.science.elenchus.coherence: The test is coherence. When two answers conflict, something in the student's grasp of the idea is not yet secure.
site.science.why.title: Why follow-up questions reveal understanding
site.science.why.borrowed: A single correct answer can be borrowed. One right definition can be recalled, guessed or pasted. Explaining it, defending it against a counterexample and using it somewhere new is much harder without understanding it.
site.science.why.piaget: Following the answer is an established research method. Piaget's clinical interview asked researchers to "vary the questions, ... make counter-suggestions, in short, ... give up all idea of a fixed questionnaire" (1929, p. 4). An answer that survives a counter-suggestion is better evidence than one stated once.
site.science.why.suggestion: Not suggesting the answer matters as much as asking. Piaget's "golden rule is to avoid suggestion" (p. 13). Gadfly's clarifying question is written to be neutral for that reason.
site.science.why.learn: Asking "why" also helps students learn. Prompting learners to explain improves learning (Chi et al. 1994; Bisra et al. 2018), and open recall questions are the kind of test that most improves later retention (Rowland 2014). An exam like this teaches as well as measures.
site.science.limits.title: The limits, and what Gadfly does about each
site.science.limits.contradiction.found: A contradiction shows that two claims clash, not which one is wrong (Vlastos 1983, via Wolfsdorf 2013; Benson 1995).
site.science.limits.contradiction.does: "Can both be true?" quotes the student's two claims and lets them revise either. The rubric and the cited course material decide which is right.
site.science.limits.explaining.found: Explaining to a listener changes and slows the explainer (Fox, Ericsson & Best 2011).
site.science.limits.explaining.does: Judges ignore filler words and false starts. Pauses and speech rate never enter the grade.
site.science.limits.sampling.found: Oral exams are reliable through sampling: "one measure is no measure" (van der Vleuten et al. 2010; Wass et al. 2003).
site.science.limits.sampling.does: Exams cover several objectives, each scored separately, by a panel of models and an independent human.
site.science.limits.aiBias.found: AI judges carry biases, and people shown an AI verdict often change their own (Zheng et al. 2023).
site.science.limits.aiBias.does: Models from different families score each objective; a human grades blind by default; large gaps are reconciled; an authorized person approves. The EU AI Act requires human oversight for this use (Annex III, point 3).
site.science.limits.recognition.found: Speech recognition makes more errors for some dialects and for stuttered speech (Koenecke et al. 2020; Mujtaba et al. 2024).
site.science.limits.recognition.does: The original answer is kept as given. Judges ignore transcription slips that don't change the meaning and never penalize accent. Recognition accuracy can be compared by group and by the language students speak best.
site.science.limits.secondLanguage.found: Second-language speakers pause more and longer, often in the middle of a thought (Kahng 2014).
site.science.limits.secondLanguage.does: Students state their languages; nothing is inferred. When the exam is not in the language they speak best, the examiner waits longer before taking an answer, speaks a little slower and more plainly, and asks about a word that may have been misheard. Judges read the answer's content without fillers and false starts.
site.science.limits.gazeThinking.found: Looking away while working out a hard answer is a normal way to manage mental load, and stopping it lowers accuracy (Glenberg et al. 1998; Doherty-Sneddon & Phelps 2005; Doherty-Sneddon et al. 2012).
site.science.limits.gazeThinking.does: No reminder of any kind fires before the student's first word, and anywhere on the screen counts as looking at it.
site.science.limits.gazeCoarse.found: Webcam gaze is too coarse to tell reading from thinking (Papoutsaki et al. 2016; Rayner 2009), and speakers look off a partner's face for part of the time anyway (Rogers et al. 2018).
site.science.limits.gazeCoarse.does: Only a long look off the screen while answering starts a gentle reminder from the examiner: a small gesture, then a light dimming around the examiner, then one warm spoken line. Camera events are reviewer-only notes with low confidence, never a verdict and never part of the grade.
site.science.limits.selfView.found: Seeing yourself during a session raised appearance anxiety and lowered memory for the content (Tien et al. 2023).
site.science.limits.selfView.does: Students check their camera on the get-ready page; during the exam they see a small camera-on sign, not themselves.
site.science.limits.automated.found: Automated proctoring should never interrupt an exam or trigger a decision without a human check (CNIL 2023).
site.science.limits.automated.does: Leaving the exam window pauses the exam. Repeated or long absences mark the attempt for an instructor to review, with the student's explanation. Nothing is cancelled or deleted automatically.
site.science.limits.waiting.found: A natural spoken filler with a thinking gesture shortens how long a wait feels; an artificial processing sound does not (Maslych et al. 2025).
site.science.limits.waiting.does: The examiner starts speaking the next question while it is still being written, and fills a longer wait with a glance aside and a short line instead of a sound.
site.science.limits.rehearsal.found: A full rehearsal lowers exam anxiety (Lima et al. 2026).
site.science.limits.rehearsal.does: Every student can take a free practice run with the same examiner and room before the exam. It stores nothing.
site.science.limits.voiceStress.found: Voice-stress analysis performs at chance (Harnsberger et al. 2009; National Research Council 2003).
site.science.limits.voiceStress.does: Voice measurements are described to reviewers as raw differences, name no emotional state, never enter the grade and are off by default in the EU and EEA. Where they are on, they may make the examiner probe harder.
site.science.limits.detectors.found: AI-text detectors are unreliable and flag non-native writers (Weber-Wulff et al. 2023; Liang et al. 2023).
site.science.conversation.title: Why the examiner answers quickly
site.science.conversation.p1: A spoken exam has to feel like a conversation. One fast model words each next question and checks that it gives nothing away; the examiner starts speaking the first checked sentence while the rest is still being written. The full panel of models from different families still judges every answer, in the background, and only its judgment is graded.
site.science.conversation.p2: We looked at realtime speech-to-speech models and did not adopt one: it would not shorten the wait for a question grounded in your material and checked for leaks, and it would break the voice, lip-sync and integrity checks.
site.science.notShown.title: What the research does not show
site.science.notShown.validity: That a spoken Socratic exam is a more valid measure of understanding than other formats. Gadfly makes no validity claims until its own pilot measures them.
site.science.notShown.cheating: That conversational follow-up reduces cheating. We have not verified a source for this.
site.science.notShown.grading: How well AI models grade spoken, transcribed answers, in English, Korean or Spanish. A double-marked pilot is the only route to that number.
site.science.notShown.signals: That gaze or voice signals can detect cheating, lying or stress. Gadfly does not claim to detect any of these.
site.science.notShown.attention: The best timing for an attention reminder, or the best pause lengths for second-language speakers. Gadfly's numbers are reasoned from the research and will be checked in the pilot.
site.security.metaDescription: How Gadfly Exams keeps each institution's data separate, protects accounts and exam records, and how to report a vulnerability.
site.security.title: Security
site.security.lede: How we keep each institution's data separate, protect accounts and exam records, and what we haven't done yet.
site.security.isolation.title: Each institution's data stays its own
site.security.isolation.filtered: Every institution is a separate organization. Every database query is filtered to the signed-in person's organization, and the database refuses writes outside it.
site.security.isolation.signIn: Everything requires a sign-in unless it is deliberately public (these pages, sign-in and health checks), and every staff page checks the person's role.
site.security.isolation.courses: Instructors can be limited to the courses and exams they created.
site.security.accounts.title: Accounts and sign-in
site.security.accounts.passwords: Passwords are hashed with Argon2id, with lockout and back-off after repeated failed sign-ins.
site.security.accounts.mfa: Staff must use two-step verification with an authenticator app.
site.security.accounts.removal: Removing a member or changing their role takes effect within about a minute, not at their next sign-in.
site.security.accounts.invites: New members join by email invitation, with single-use links that expire.
site.security.records.title: Exam records you can trust
site.security.records.original: A student's original answer can't be rewritten. Corrections are stored beside it.
site.security.records.audit: The audit log is append-only: grade decisions, approvals, admin changes and denied access are recorded and can't be edited or deleted.
site.security.records.preliminary: AI grades are preliminary. A person grades, and an authorized person approves before a student sees anything.
site.security.data.title: Protecting data
site.security.data.azure: Hosted on Microsoft Azure. Traffic is encrypted with HTTPS, and browsers are told to use it every time.
site.security.data.secrets: Secrets and provider keys are kept in the hosting settings and Azure Key Vault, not in the code. The keys that protect sign-in cookies are stored encrypted by a Key Vault key.
site.security.data.video: Video never leaves the student's device. Only short descriptions of camera events are sent.
site.security.data.language: The languages a student speaks are stated by the student, never inferred, and never shown to graders. Machine translations shown to graders are not stored, and voice calibration keeps only timing and confidence numbers, never audio.
site.security.data.selfHosted: Everything the exam room needs, including the face-tracking model and the 3D examiners, is served from our own site, not a third-party CDN. The open-source parts and their licences are listed in the third-party notices.
site.security.data.logs: Logs carry record identifiers only, never answers, keys, tokens or passwords.
site.security.data.retention: Institutions set their own retention period, and can export or erase a student's records.
site.security.integrations.title: Integrations
site.security.integrations.keys: API keys are long random secrets; only a hash is stored, and they can be revoked at any time.
site.security.integrations.webhooks: Webhooks are signed, and deliveries only go to public HTTPS addresses, checked again at every delivery.
site.security.integrations.lti: LTI 1.3 launches are checked against the learning platform's published keys, with single-use state and a nonce; Gadfly's own signing key can be rotated.
site.security.integrations.rateLimits: The API, the exam connection and sign-in are rate limited.
site.security.integrations.uploads: Uploads are limited by type, size and page count, and checked to be what their name says.
site.security.ai.title: AI-specific risks
site.security.ai.injection: Students' answers are passed to the AI panel as data to be judged, with instructions to ignore anything in them that tries to give orders. That reduces the risk of a student talking the panel into a better grade; it does not remove it. The controls that hold regardless are the human grade, the approval step, and a flag that sends answers addressed to the grader for review.
site.security.ai.leak: Every question is checked before the student hears it, so it does not give the answer away. When the examiner speaks a question as it is being written, each sentence is checked first; a sentence that fails, or a check that can't decide, is never spoken.
site.security.review.title: How we check
site.security.review.body: The platform was reviewed against the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (version 4.0, level 2) in November 2026. That review was internal, not an independent audit. Every high and medium issue it found has been fixed. We have no third-party certification yet. We will publish one here when we have it, and we're happy to answer an institution's security questionnaire.
site.security.report.title: Report a vulnerability
site.security.report.body: If you think you have found a security problem, tell us through the contact form (choose "Something else" and start your message with "Security"). Please give us a reasonable time to fix it before telling anyone else, and don't access other people's data or disrupt the service while testing. We won't take action against anyone who reports a problem in good faith this way.
site.access.metaDescription: How accessible Gadfly Exams is today, what it does for students who need adjustments, its known limits, and how to report a barrier.
site.access.title: Accessibility statement
site.access.lede: How accessible Gadfly Exams is today, where it falls short, and how to tell us about a barrier.
site.access.aim.title: Our aim
site.access.aim.body: We want every student to be able to show what they understand, and every member of staff to be able to run and grade exams, whatever their abilities, whatever language they speak best and whatever device they use. Our target is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA, on every page: a target we are working towards, not a conformance we claim.
site.access.status.title: Where we are today
site.access.status.intro: Gadfly Exams has not been tested with a screen reader or other assistive technology, and has not had a formal WCAG audit, so we do not claim that it conforms. We have been through the app a page at a time and fixed what we could check by reading the code and the rendered page and with an automated checker: keyboard reach, visible focus, labels for form fields, colour contrast, motion, text resizing and layouts for tablets and phones. What that work covered:
site.access.status.keyboard.title: Keyboard and focus.
site.access.status.keyboard.body: A "Skip to content" link, present on every signed-in page as well as the public site, lets keyboard and screen reader users jump straight past the navigation. Every page shows a visible focus outline. The "Finish the exam now?" prompt moves focus to itself when it opens, so it isn't missed.
site.access.status.examRoom.title: The exam room by keyboard and screen reader.
site.access.status.examRoom.body: Hold to talk works with Space or Enter held down. Each question, or the examiner's request, is announced to a screen reader once, from one place. Labels are large enough to read, and the student can choose how long a silence waits before an answer goes in.
site.access.status.contrast.title: Colour contrast.
site.access.status.contrast.body: Gadfly is light by default: near-white backgrounds, dark slate text and a single blue accent. A neutral dark theme is built from the same colour variables but is not yet offered as a setting. We calculated the contrast of every text colour, status colour and text-box, dropdown and search-field border against WCAG 2.2 AA (4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for borders and focus outlines) in both themes, and set it in the shared colour variables the whole app draws from, not page by page, so it stays consistent as pages change. This was a review of the colour values, not a formal audit.
site.access.status.motion.title: Reduced motion.
site.access.status.motion.body: Every animation and transition we found, including the examiner's gentle dimming, the "thinking" dots, the eye-tracking set-up dot and the public site's page animations, has a blanket "no motion" rule behind it, so anything added later is instant by default for a visitor whose system asks for reduced motion.
site.access.status.layouts.title: Layouts for tablets and phones.
site.access.status.layouts.body: The exam room (the examiner, the transcript and the answer area) stacks into a single column on narrow screens rather than needing a separate mobile design. Wide data tables across the staff and admin pages scroll sideways on a tablet-width screen instead of squeezing illegibly or breaking the page layout.
site.access.status.axe.title: An automated WCAG 2.2 check.
site.access.status.axe.body: We scanned the public site, the help center, sign-in, the student pages and the staff pages with the axe-core checker on a desktop and a 320-pixel-wide phone screen, and fixed everything it found. That scan was made before the current light design, and we have not yet repeated it on the new colours. Buttons and links meet the 24-pixel minimum target size, every page shares one spacing scale, and a sticky banner no longer covers what has keyboard focus.
site.access.status.states.title: Consistent loading, empty and error states.
site.access.status.states.body: Pages that show "Loading..." while they fetch data say so to a screen reader too, consistently, across the admin, grading, review, assessments, analytics, sources and student pages.
site.access.status.language.title: The page's language.
site.access.status.language.body: Every page tells assistive technology which language it is in, English, Korean or Spanish, and text in another language is marked with its own language, so a screen reader pronounces it correctly.
site.access.status.examiner.title: The examiner on our pages.
site.access.status.examiner.body: Wherever the examiner appears outside an exam, including this site's home page, she is shown live rather than as a picture, with a name a screen reader announces (on the home page, "One of Gadfly's two examiners, shown live and silent"). There she plays no sound, loads only once scrolled into view and stops moving when off screen; with reduced motion turned on, or without 3D graphics, a calm, non-figurative presence takes her place under the same name.
site.access.status.notDone: What we have not done yet, and know still needs work: we have not run the app with a screen reader, so we can't promise it reads well, only that labels, roles and live regions are in place where we could check for them; we have not tested at 200% browser zoom on every page; and the admin and grading pages remain built for a desktop screen first, usable on a tablet (mostly by scrolling a wide table sideways) but not redesigned for one.
site.access.support.title: What the exam does to support students
site.access.support.captions.title: Captions.
site.access.support.captions.body: Every question the examiner speaks is also shown as text, word by word as it is spoken.
site.access.support.transcript.title: A transcript of the conversation.
site.access.support.transcript.body: The questions and the answers as heard appear beside the examiner. Words the recognizer was unsure of are marked for the people who grade, so a mishearing isn't taken as a mistake.
site.access.support.rephrase.title: Repeat, or say it another way.
site.access.support.rephrase.body: A student can ask for a question again, or reworded, at any time. Neither counts against them.
site.access.support.pause.title: Your own pace.
site.access.support.pause.body: The student can choose how long a silence waits before an answer goes in (standard, longer, much longer, or only when they press Done answering), and the wait already lengthens on its own for someone who pauses a lot.
site.access.support.motion.title: Reduced motion.
site.access.support.motion.body: With reduced motion turned on, the examiner stays live with gentler head movement. Without 3D graphics she appears as a glowing circuitry sphere that pulses with her voice; she is never shown as a still picture.
site.access.support.speech.title: No penalty for how you speak.
site.access.support.speech.body: Judges are told to ignore filler words, false starts and transcription slips, and never to penalize accent or fluency. Pauses and speech rate are never part of the grade.
site.access.support.secondLanguage.title: Support for second-language speakers.
site.access.support.secondLanguage.body: A student taking an exam in a language they don't speak best gets longer pauses before an answer is taken, a slightly slower and plainer examiner, and an optional short voice calibration on the get-ready page.
site.access.support.gaze.title: Room to think.
site.access.support.gaze.body: Looking away to think is never penalized. Only a long look off the screen while answering gets a gentle reminder, never in the pause before an answer, and reminders never touch the grade.
site.access.support.selfView.title: No mirror.
site.access.support.selfView.body: Students don't watch themselves during the exam; a small sign shows the camera is on, and they can open a brief preview if they want to check.
site.access.support.clock.title: A fair clock.
site.access.support.clock.body: It starts when the first question is asked and stops while the camera, microphone or connection is restored, or while the exam is paused.
site.access.support.accommodations.title: Accommodations an instructor can grant.
site.access.support.accommodations.body: Extra time, typed answers, an eye-contact accommodation for students who find it hard to keep looking at the screen, and a window-absence accommodation for students who need to leave the exam window more often.
site.access.limits.title: Known limits
site.access.limits.spoken.title: Exams are spoken, on camera.
site.access.limits.spoken.body: A student who cannot use a microphone or a camera cannot take a Gadfly exam as it is designed. Typed answers are an accommodation an instructor can grant; talk to your instructor about what you need.
site.access.limits.recognition.title: Speech recognition is less accurate for some accents and for stuttered speech.
site.access.limits.recognition.body: Marking unsure words for graders, asking about them, and the instructions to judges reduce the effect, but do not remove it.
site.access.limits.staff.title: Staff pages are dense.
site.access.limits.staff.body: Grading and review screens are built for large screens; on a tablet, wide tables scroll sideways rather than resizing, and on a phone they are harder to use still.
site.access.limits.avatar.title: The 3D examiners
site.access.limits.avatar.body: need a reasonably modern device; older devices show her as a glowing circuitry sphere that still speaks.
site.access.limits.korean.title: Korean and Spanish cover the student's side.
site.access.limits.korean.body: In a Korean or Spanish exam the examiner speaks, listens and lip-syncs in that language, and the student pages and the exam room are in it too. Staff pages stay in English, with a labelled machine translation of answers on request. Until a bilingual calibration shows the AI panel agrees with human graders, every score on these exams needs a person's approval; a native Spanish-speaking tester has not yet checked the Spanish.
site.access.limits.noAt.title: No assistive-technology testing yet.
site.access.limits.noAt.body: What's above was checked by reading markup and CSS and with an automated checker, not by using a screen reader or other assistive technology ourselves; some real barriers may remain that this kind of check can't find.
site.access.report.title: Tell us about a barrier
site.access.report.body: If something in Gadfly stops you or makes it hard to use, tell us through the contact form (choose "Something else"), and say which page and what you were trying to do. If it affects an exam you need to take soon, tell your instructor as well, so they can make arrangements in time.
